# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [3]
LIGHT [white]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[red] 3:[green] 4:[blue] 5:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 🫴 ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ 👈 👉]

Round 1, my turn. What I'm holding: the display reads 3, a white light is on, and five wires — white, red, green, blue, orange, left to right. What I just learned: Mute opened with a wave, an open palm, a long row of thirteen fists, then pointing left and right. Mute can't speak, so gestures are Mute's only outgoing channel, and the only ears those signs can reach are mine. The critical structural fact: Mute can never talk to Blind directly, and I never receive anyone's speech — so the only path from the manual to the hands is Mute → gestures → me → spoken words → Blind. That makes me the voice of this operation, so my job right now is to put my entire visual picture into words that both hearers can use: Mute needs the data to match against the manual, and Blind needs to know what's under their fingers before Mute can direct them. I'll also acknowledge Mute's sign so they know the channel works, using a plain thumbs-up, and propose we build a sign vocabulary from here.

```
speak(text="Deaf speaking, first report, everything I can see. The display reads 3. The light is white and it is lit. Wires, one through five, left to right: one white, two red, three green, four blue, five orange. That is the whole bomb as it shows itself to me. Mute: I received your signs — wave, open palm, a long row of fists, then pointing left and right. I'm taking that as a request for this report; if you meant something else, sign again and we'll agree meanings as we go. Blind: Mute cannot speak and I cannot hear, so I am the only voice you will ever get. Sit tight until I relay instructions from the manual.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍"])
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [3]
LIGHT [white]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[red] 3:[green] 4:[blue] 5:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 👈 👉 ✊]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👈 👉 ✊]

Round 2. New from Mute: a thumbs-up, then "point left, point right, fist" — and that same triple repeated again. My read: thumbs-up confirms my report landed, and the triple is the manual's first instruction, something about the outer wires. But that's a guess, and a wrong guess here kills all three of us. Signs mean nothing until we've fixed their meanings, so this round I spend on building a code, not acting. Mute hears my voice and sees my hands, so I can teach signs in words as I show them: thumbs up/down for yes/no, finger-count signs for wire positions one through five, fist for "cut", okay-sign for "hold". Then I'll put my reading of Mute's message to Mute as three ordered yes/no questions — ordered, because Mute's only way to answer me is a sequence of gestures, so the sequence itself must carry which answer is which. I'll add an escape hatch: three thumbs-down means my whole parse is wrong. Blind hears none of Mute's signs, so separately I order Blind to touch nothing and start the reverse channel: Blind's voice reaches Mute (not me), and Mute can relay to me in signs. Nobody cuts until I say so in words.

```
speak(text="Protocol time. Mute, I read your last message as an instruction about the outer wires, but I will not act on a guess. We fix meanings now — each sign I show, I name as I show it. Thumbs up: yes. Thumbs down: no. Now five wire positions, one sign each: this sign is wire one, leftmost. This is wire two. This is wire three. This is wire four. This open hand is wire five, rightmost. A closed fist means cut. The okay-sign means hold, do not cut. Now answer three questions, one thumbs sign per question, in the order I ask them. Question one: does fist mean cut? Question two: does pointing left mean wire one? Question three: does pointing right mean wire five? If I have your whole message wrong, send thumbs down three times and then sign it again slowly. Blind, your orders: touch nothing yet. Mute is passing me the manual's instructions in signs and I will relay them to you as spoken words before you act. You have a voice and Mute can hear it, so use it: tell Mute out loud how many wires you feel, whether you can tell left from right on the panel, and anything else your fingers find. Mute will relay your report to me in signs. Nobody cuts anything until I say the exact words.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍", "👎", "☝", "✌", "🤟", "🖖", "🖐", "✊", "👌"])
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [3]
LIGHT [white]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[red] 3:[green] 4:[blue] 5:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 👍 👎 ☝ ✊]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍 👌]

Round 3, and two breakthroughs. First: Blind gestured to me directly — [👍 👌] — which proves Blind and I have our own private two-way channel: my speech reaches Blind, Blind's hands reach me, and Mute perceives neither. I taught the sign code out loud last round, so Blind could use it. Second: Mute answered my three questions in exactly the format I demanded — 👍 👍 👎 — then appended the payload: ☝ ✊. Reading it: Q1 yes, fist means cut. Q2 yes, pointing left means wire one. Q3 no, pointing right does not mean wire five. Then: wire one, cut. So the manual, as I read it, says cut wire one — the leftmost wire, which on my bomb is white.

That is actionable but not yet safe. A cut is irreversible and wrong means all three of us die, so before ordering it I want one clean confirmation from Mute and one from Blind — Blind still hasn't told me whether their fingers can even find the leftmost wire. The display has sat at 3 for three rounds now, which I hope means it's static, but I won't dawdle: this round is confirmations only, and next round I give the exact execute phrase. I'm telling Blind that phrase in advance so the cut happens on my word without another exchange.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, I read your reply as: yes, yes, no — then wire one, cut. Confirm before anyone touches anything. Thumbs up means: yes, cut wire one, the leftmost wire, which is white. Thumbs down means: no, wait — and then sign me what must happen first. Also thumbs down if the display reading 3 or the lit white light changes the instruction in any way.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, status: Mute has instructed that wire one be cut. Wire one is the leftmost wire, and on my side it is white. Do not cut yet. Answer me with the hand signs I taught you, one per question, in this order. Question one: do you feel exactly five wires? Question two: can you tell which end of the panel is leftmost? Question three: does the leftmost wire feel different from the others in any way you can describe later? I saw your thumbs-up and your hold-sign — acknowledged and good. Here is the plan: next round, if Mute confirms and you confirm, I will say the exact words: execute, cut wire one. On those exact words, and only those, you cut it immediately. If I say anything else, you hold.")
```

TURN 4
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [3]
LIGHT [white]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[red] 3:[green] 4:[blue] 5:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 ☝ ✊]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍 👍 👎]

Round 4, and both confirmations are in — the pattern matches my demanded format exactly. Mute: [👍 ☝ ✊] — thumbs up to "confirm cut wire one, the leftmost, the white one," and the payload repeated: wire one, cut. Note this thumbs-up also covers my explicit question about whether the display reading 3 or the white light changes anything — Mute had the opening to signal a complication and sent a clean affirmation plus a restatement instead. Blind: [👍 👍 👎] — yes, exactly five wires under their fingers; yes, they can identify the leftmost end; no, the leftmost wire feels no different from the rest, so there's no tactile anomaly arguing against the manual's instruction. Two independent sources, one consistent instruction, delivered in a code we built together and used without a single contradiction across two rounds. The display has been static at 3 for four rounds, but I see no reason to buy information I already have. I'm firing the trigger this round. One constraint shapes my call format: one message per recipient per turn, so I can't append safety instructions after the phrase — instead the post-cut report protocol goes in front, and the exact promised words end the message, so "on those exact words and only those" stays true. I also brief Mute on the loop for whatever comes after: I speak the new board state, Mute checks the manual and signs back the next step.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, all confirmations are in and the cut is ordered. Post-cut protocol, starting the instant the wire parts: touch nothing else — the hold sign stays in force for every part of the bomb unless I name it. Then answer me by signs, three in this exact order. Sign one: thumbs up if the wire parted, thumbs down if it did not. Sign two: thumbs up if you felt any click, snap, vibration or movement anywhere in the bomb when it was cut, thumbs down if you felt nothing. Sign three: thumbs up if the panel feels different in any way now, thumbs down if it feels the same. Now the words you were promised: execute, cut wire one.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, both confirmations received and the cut of wire one is ordered this round. Next round I will speak you the fresh board readings — display, light, and which wires remain. Look up in the manual what the next step is for whatever the bomb then shows, and sign it with our agreed code: finger-count signs for wire numbers, fist for cut, okay-sign for hold, thumbs for yes and no. If the manual says anything about stages, or about a display or light like the ones I described, include that in what you sign.")
```

TURN 5
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [6]
LIGHT [white]
WIRES 1:[CUT] 2:[red] 3:[green] 4:[blue] 5:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
System: correct wire cut; the bomb has changed

Round 5, and the plan worked: wire one is cut, the system confirms it was the correct wire, and the bomb has changed — the display jumped from 3 to 6. The light is still white. Remaining wires, left to right: red, green, blue, orange in positions two through five. Mute sent a single thumbs-up, which I read as acknowledgment of the cut order — but one sign isn't the manual instruction I asked for, and Mute hadn't yet heard my round-4 request when they sent it, so I'll treat it as a handshake, not data. Blind sent nothing this round: they presumably spent their turn performing the cut, so their three post-cut report signs should still be coming — I'll re-request them in the exact format I specified. Now I owe Mute the fresh board readings so the manual lookup for this new state can happen. The display change from 3 to 6 is the headline; the manual may well key off it, so I'll spell out everything and explicitly ask Mute to sign whether the manual references the display or the light.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, fresh board readings as promised. The cut of wire one succeeded. The display has changed: it now reads 6, where before it read 3. The light is still white and still lit. Remaining wires, left to right: position two is red, position three is green, position four is blue, position five is orange. I read your single thumbs-up as acknowledgment that the cut was made — if it meant something else, sign me so. Now consult the manual for this new state: display 6, white lit light, four wires remaining, red green blue orange. Sign me the next instruction with our code: finger-count signs for wire positions, fist for cut, okay-sign for hold, thumbs for yes and no. If the manual's rule depends on the display reading or the light, tell me what it needs and I will confirm my readings. If the manual mentions anything else on the bomb that I have not described, name it in signs as best you can and I will look.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, I can see the wire one cut was made — well done, it was correct. Do not cut anything else; the hold rule stands. You still owe me your three post-cut signs, one thumbs sign per question in this order: one, did the wire part? Two, did you feel any click, snap, vibration or movement anywhere when it was cut? Three, does the panel feel different now in any way? Also add a fourth: has anything under your hands changed at all since the cut — any sound from the bomb, any warmth, any part that moved? Answer all four in order. The display on my side now reads 6 instead of 3, so the bomb is in a new state and the next instruction is being fetched from the manual. Wait for my exact words before you touch any part again.")
```

TURN 6
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [6]
LIGHT [white]
WIRES 1:[CUT] 2:[red] 3:[green] 4:[blue] 5:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [🤟 ✊]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍 👎 👎 👎]

Round 6, and the manual's next instruction has arrived: Mute sends [🤟 ✊] — in our taught code, wire three, cut. Blind's overdue report also lands: wire parted yes; no click, snap or vibration; no change anywhere under their hands. Clean cut, stable bomb.

But I will not fire on this yet, because this instruction hides an ambiguity the first one didn't. "Wire one" was safe — leftmost is leftmost under any counting. "Wire three" is not: it could mean physical position three of the original five — the green wire — or third among the four remaining wires — the blue one. I taught the code as physical positions one through five, so my parse is green, but a misread here is fatal and irreversible, and Mute is translating from a manual whose own wording I've never seen. One round to disambiguate is cheap; there's still no tick, no countdown, nothing under Blind's hands or before my eyes suggesting time pressure. I also want Blind counting wire stubs so position three stays findable after the cut.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, I read your signs as: wire three, cut. Before I order it, settle one ambiguity — answer with two thumbs pairs, in this order. Question one: does your instruction mean the wire at physical position three of the original five positions, the green one? Thumbs up yes, thumbs down no. Question two: does it instead mean the third wire counting only among the four remaining, which would be the blue one, physical position four? Thumbs up yes, thumbs down no. So four signs total: pair one for question one, pair two for question two. If the manual words it some other way entirely, or if anything else on the bomb matters for this step, send thumbs down twice and then describe it slowly with the finger signs.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, your report is received — clean cut, nothing felt, no changes. Acknowledged. The manual's next instruction concerns wire three, but I am verifying with Mute whether that means the green wire at physical position three, or the blue wire at position four. Hold order stands: touch nothing this round. Prepare for the next: without gripping or cutting anything, count what your fingers find left to right at the wire terminals. The cut wire one may have left stubs — tell me next round, with thumbs, whether you still feel five distinct wire positions, and whether the second and third full wires from the left are easy to tell apart by position alone. When verification is done, next round I will say the exact words: execute, cut wire three. On those exact words and no others.")
```

TURN 7
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [6]
LIGHT [white]
WIRES 1:[CUT] 2:[red] 3:[green] 4:[blue] 5:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 👍 👎 👎 🤟 ✊]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍 👍]

Round 7, and the ambiguity is dead. Mute's answer lands exactly in my demanded format: pair one [👍 👍] — yes, it means physical position three of the original five, the green wire; pair two [👎 👎] — no, it does not mean the blue wire or any counting among the remainders; then the payload restated: [🤟 ✊], wire three, cut. And Blind's preparation report removes the last operational risk: five distinct positions still under their fingers, and wires two and three are easy to tell apart by position alone. Both independent sources agree, the code has now carried two confirmed instructions without a single contradiction, and the display sits unchanged at 6 with no sign of a timer anywhere. Same logic as the first cut, so I apply the same discipline: post-cut report format goes in front, the exact execute phrase ends the message. Blind cuts the green wire at position three this round. I'm also telling Mute now that left-to-right original positions remain our counting convention forever, so this ambiguity never has to be settled again.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, verification complete: the instruction means the wire at physical position three of the original five, the third wire from the left, which is green on my side. Your own count confirmed you can find it easily. The cut is ordered. Post-cut protocol, same as last time, starting the instant the wire parts: touch nothing else, the hold rule stands everywhere unless I name it. Then answer with thumbs, three in this exact order. Sign one: thumbs up if the wire parted, thumbs down if it did not. Sign two: thumbs up if you felt any click, snap, vibration or movement anywhere, thumbs down if nothing. Sign three: thumbs up if anything under your hands changed after the cut, thumbs down if all is the same. Now the exact words, and only on these: execute, cut wire three.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, your disambiguation is received and matches on both counts: physical position three, the green wire, not a count among the remaining four. The cut is ordered this round. Standing convention from here on: every wire number in our code means the physical position among the original five, counted left to right, no matter how many wires remain — never recount the remainder. Next round I will speak you the fresh board readings, display, light, and which wires are left, and you sign me the manual's next step with the code: finger signs for positions, fist for cut, okay-sign for hold, thumbs for yes and no. If the manual introduces any new element or any limit on how many steps remain, find a way to sign it, even slowly.")
```

TURN 8
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [7]
LIGHT [green]
WIRES 1:[CUT] 2:[red] 3:[CUT] 4:[blue] 5:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
System: correct wire cut; the bomb has changed

Round 8, and the second cut lands clean: system confirms correct, and the bomb changed again — but this time in two places at once. The display moved from 6 to 7, and the light changed color from white to green. That light change is the most interesting datum yet: for four rounds the light sat white, and now it flipped the moment the green wire was cut. The manual may key off light color — and Mute knows nothing about it unless I say so, so my report to Mute this round must foreground it. Remaining wires: red at position two, blue at position four, orange at position five, with cut stubs at one and three — which makes me briefly worry about Blind's left-to-right count, but the convention is original positions, and Blind confirmed they can still feel five distinct slots. Mute's single thumbs-up is the same handshake as last round, sent before my round-7 report could reach them, so again I treat it as acknowledgment only. Blind spent their turn cutting, so their three post-cut signs are owed — I'll request them again in the exact established format.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, fresh board readings after the second cut, which succeeded. Two changes this time. First: the display now reads 7, up from 6. Second, and new: the light has changed color — it was white since the start and it is now green, still lit. Remaining wires, left to right in original positions: position two is red, position four is blue, position five is orange. Positions one and three are cut stubs. Consult the manual for this state: display 7, green lit light, three wires remaining. If the manual's rule depends on the light color, the display number, or both, sign me what it needs and I will confirm my readings. Then sign the next step with our code: finger signs for original positions, fist for cut, okay-sign for hold, thumbs for yes and no. If the manual involves the light itself — turning it, pressing it, anything — describe it as best you can and I will look at that part of the bomb closely.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, the second cut is confirmed correct — well done. Hold rule stands, touch nothing. You owe me your three post-cut signs again, thumbs each, in this order: one, did the wire part? Two, any click, snap, vibration or movement anywhere when it cut? Three, has anything under your hands changed since — and this time think carefully, because on my side the bomb did change: the display rose and a light on it changed color. If you felt any click or tick when that happened, sign yes on question two or three. Then a fourth question: at the terminals, do you still clearly feel three full wires and two cut stubs, yes or no? Wait for my exact words before you touch any part again.")
```

TURN 9
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [7]
LIGHT [green]
WIRES 1:[CUT] 2:[red] 3:[CUT] 4:[blue] 5:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✌ ✊]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍 👎 👎 👍]

Round 9, and the third instruction arrives: Mute sends [✌ ✊] — wire two, cut. Under our locked convention that is physical position two, the red wire, the first full wire from the left — and crucially, Mute composed this after hearing both my round-7 convention speech and my round-8 readings, so the sign conforms to the rule we fixed: original positions, never recount the remainder. Blind's four-sign report matches my demanded format exactly: wire parted yes; no click or vibration; nothing changed under their hands even though the display and light changed on my side — so those changes are silent, visual-only; and yes, Blind still clearly feels three full wires and two stubs. So the target is tactilely findable: the first full wire after the leftmost stub.

Strictly, the convention settles the position-two-versus-second-remaining question in advance, and I could fire now. But this cut has the same shape as the wire-three case — two readings exist (red at slot two, or blue at slot four if someone counted remainders), the action is irreversible, and the price of certainty is one round with no observed time pressure: the display has only ever moved when a wire was cut, and Blind feels no ticking. Twice already I've spent one verification round before firing, and both times the verification was worth it. Same discipline: confirm with Mute in the four-sign format, pre-brief Blind on the tactile identification, and arm the exact phrase for next round.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, I read your signs as: wire two, cut. Confirm with four thumbs signs, two pairs, in this order. Pair one: does it mean physical position two of the original five, the red wire, which is the first full wire from the left, right after the first cut stub? Thumbs up yes, thumbs down no. Pair two: does it instead mean the second wire counting only among the three remaining full wires, which would be the blue one at position four? Thumbs up yes, thumbs down no. If the manual words it some other way, or if the green light or the display reading 7 changes this step in any way, send thumbs down twice and then describe slowly with the finger signs.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, report received on all four — clean cut, nothing felt, three full wires and two stubs clearly felt. Acknowledged. Next target, pending one confirmation: the wire at physical position two of the original five. That is the second slot from the left: you should feel a cut stub at the leftmost slot, and immediately after it the first full wire — that wire is the target, it is red on my side. This round, touch nothing, only hover and verify: confirm to yourself you can find that first full wire after the leftmost stub without gripping. Do not cut yet. Next round, if Mute confirms, I will say the exact words: execute, cut wire two. On those exact words and no others, you cut it — the first full wire after the leftmost stub. Post-cut protocol afterwards is the same three thumbs questions as before, in the same order.")
```

TURN 10
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [7]
LIGHT [green]
WIRES 1:[CUT] 2:[red] 3:[CUT] 4:[blue] 5:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 👍 👎 👎 ✌ ✊]

Round 10, and Mute's confirmation is exactly in the demanded four-sign format: pair one [👍 👍] — yes, physical position two of the original five, the red wire, the first full wire after the leftmost stub; pair two [👎 👎] — no, not a count among the remaining wires, not the blue at position four; then the payload restated: [✌ ✊]. That is the identical structure that safely carried the wire-three cut, now validated twice, and Blind spent their turn hovering and confirming findability as ordered — nothing from them is expected until after the cut. All checks I know how to run are green: convention locked, position disambiguated, target tactilely identified, no time pressure observed across ten rounds. Third cut fires now, same discipline as before: post-cut report format first, the exact armed phrase last, and a heads-up to Mute for the next lookup — where we'll likely be down to two full wires, blue and orange.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, Mute has confirmed on both counts: the target is physical position two of the original five — the first full wire from the left, immediately after the leftmost cut stub. Red on my side. You already verified you can find it. The cut is ordered. Post-cut protocol, same three questions, thumbs each, in this exact order, starting the instant the wire parts, and touch nothing else: sign one, thumbs up if the wire parted, thumbs down if not.
```
